article.title: Healthcare workers respond to a broken system by unionizing
article.author: Dennis Kosuth
article.content: C hicago is seeing a burst of unionization amongst registered nurses – and it has become infectious, in the best sense of that word. In May of 2026, 77 percent of nurses at Rush University Medical Center (RUMC) voted in favor of joining the National Nurses Organizing Committee (NNOC). The 1,700 nurses at RUMC are now part of National Nurses United (NNU), a union that represents 225,000 nurses in healthcare settings across the United States. NNU was founded by a merger of nursing unions in 2009 and, in the past 17 years,has grown considerably from its initial strength of 150,000. The latest victory for NNOC took place in the first week of November when nurses who work for Endeavor Health at Edward Hospital in suburban Naperville, voted by a margin of 65 percent in favor of joining the union. By adding another 1,200 nurses to the Chicagoland area, NNOC now represents over 10,000 members in the region. Nurses at Chicago’s Saint Mary of Nazareth Hospital voted 96 percent in favor of unionizing in June of 2026 – days after going on a one-day strike six days before the vote had even occurred- over the unlawful termination of nurses who were advocating for having a collective voice in their workplace. St. Mary Hospital was acquired by Prime Healthcare in March of 2025, and nurses were motivated to take action following drastic changes they experienced in patient care, following cost-cutting measures taken by Prime to boost their bottom line. Nurses at St. Mary struck again for one day on September 3. On September 15, nurses at Olympia Fields Hospital in suburban Chicago, also owned by Prime Healthcare, went on a one-day strike, also voting with an 82 percent margin to join the union about a week afterwards, adding another 400 nurses to NNOC. In early December, 2,400 nurses at four hospitals in the northern Chicago suburbs owned by Endeavor will have an opportunity to vote to organize with Teamsters Union Local 743. Across the United States, there are almost 4.5 million registered nurses, and about one in five of them are in unions – double the overall unionization rate of workers in this country. There are various factors at play behind these statistics, with the most notable ones being a response to chronic understaffing, post-COVID pandemic exhaustion, and the leverage that comes with the relatively higher job security that nurses have. I am a NNOC member, a nurse who works part-time at Cook County’s Stroger hospital, and recently was in conversation with three nurses from St. Mary Hospital and one nurse from RUMC. They had all led successful campaigns to unionize their hospitals with NNOC in the spring of 2026. The testimony of these nurses is useful for understanding what is pushing nurses to organize themselves, the challenges they are confronting in these campaigns, and what the future holds for healthcare workers fighting for justice. Mary, a nurse who works at RUMC, reported on how her coworkers joined the organizing campaign at St. Mary, on the heels of the RUMC vote to join NNOC. She said, “The most inspiring thing was seeing nurses come together for St. Mary’s. It came at the perfect time for us because everyone was so hyped up and excited and ready to jump into action. Seeing people [at RUMC] commit the time, not just for ourselves, but for other nurses in the community to make all nurses in Chicago, and the country, to make work better for them – was really inspiring.” Working conditions were a major driver of nurse unionization. Richard, a nurse at St. Mary, described what motivated him to organize after Prime took over. “Things just got worse and worse. One of the things that happened is my coworker got his ribs broken and he got a black eye from being beaten really badly by a patient because we weren’t staffed properly. I just wanted to be able to have them give us a proper amount of staff under whatever circumstances we have, rather than just applying to some basic rule of one staff to six patients.” Patient safety was a big concern for Jesús, also a nurse at St. Mary, as the employer didn’t want to have “sitters,” someone to watch patients to prevent falls. His unit has “a lot of geriatric dementia patients, and Prime wanted them to be without a sitter, and they were pushing us to admit these patients without one. You can’t really say that patients need a sitter right away, but you’ve seen enough falls and enough adverse complications from falls to know who needs one. They wouldn’t listen to us because the care that patients need, they’re not going to get it, because Prime is trying to squeeze as much juice out of a lemon.” When Mary from RUSH worked as an agency nurse at a unionized hospital, it gave her a glimpse into what conditions might be like. “Nurses wanted to stay and make the hospital a better place to work as opposed to, ‘I’m going to quit and go wherever I feel respected,’ because they do feel respected and appreciated there. Their compensation was on par with other hospitals in the area, and the culture was just more collaborative. Keeping experienced nurses at the bedside was only going to do good things for patients.” Prime Healthcare is a privately held for-profit system, which generates billions of dollars in revenue from its systems across the country, and its assets have only increased since acquiring six more hospitals in the Chicago area. Jesús, who was fired by Prime for advocating for unionization, is directly experiencing their wrath and the wealth they have at their disposal to resist the union. “They have that money. It’s nothing to them because they make billions of dollars off the backs of the patients as well as us.” He continued by saying, “They’re just like, ‘you don’t need any hallway monitors,’ because it just saves them money. They just think, ‘you can take these two patients,’ and they don’t have to pay two nurses. They don’t think about the safety and the potential complications of adverse effects.” Brenda, a nurse at St. Mary, described what provoked nurses to take action. “We decided to go on strike because Prime kept retaliating against our colleagues. They had said that they were going to stop. The day that we received the news of an election date, Prime called two more nurses and left a voicemail that they were terminated because they were, according to Prime, ‘trespassing.’ This was completely false because that’s when we were leafleting, and we had a federal law protecting the right to do that. That’s what made us say, ‘you know what? This is enough.” Richard added, “Our strike was before we had a union, which is unheard of. When our coworkers got fired, a lot of people became very angry. Someone asked me: what was the secret of how you unionized? What was the secret to getting support? The secret to getting support was our company and their war on nurses. A lot of the people became very upset. We won by 96 percent because the company made a lot of nurses very angry.” Even at a so-called non-profit hospital like RUMC, whose policies and practices are nowhere near as nakedly offensive as Prime’s, nurses still overwhelmingly supported unionization. Mary describes how her coworkers saw organizing a union as “having power, having a seat at the table. Having a say in what’s happening to us, what’s happening to our patients. Having a say in our compensation, in our benefits, in our healthcare, in our tuition reimbursement, because that could change whenever Rush wants it. Those benefits could go away at any minute, the only way we can actually secure those is in a contract.” The underlying factor of who ultimately controls the workplace surfaced in both for-profit and non-profit systems. During the unionization campaign, RUMC countered that management had open channels of communication with nurses. Mary described what it looked like: “The hospital’s stance was, ‘We have this great shared governance model. Nurses have so much say. Here are some of the things we’ve taken into account. Here are some of the changes we’ve made.” There was a big push for doing Zoom calls to answer questions, but those questions were very filtered, and we lost our opportunity to talk. Then we lost our cameras. People saw how much Rush was restricting open dialogue, and they were like, “okay.” Jesús described organizing for justice at St. Mary in this way. “It’s a very common issue, and it doesn’t matter what you do, if you’re an Amazon worker or you work in a kitchen, you work. There’s always that power struggle between people trying to make money and you trying to do your job. It’s about the working class coming together.” Brenda reported how workers across different units in the hospital joined together. “It was inspiring how we started to connect unit to unit. Before, ICU [intensive care unit] and emergency room, they are different worlds. In the ICU we’re like, ‘ER is just sending all their patients out to us.’ After getting to know everyone, talking to everyone during the meetings, as well as psychiatry, medical-surgical units… it’s like little towns, right? Getting everyone connected and on the same page, that was one of the best things that we saw.” Jesús went on to describe the importance of links between healthcare workers and their community and how unionization will help stabilize care for patients. “St. Mary has been here a long time. I’ve met people who were like, ‘I was born in this hospital,’ and they have no other place to go, they’re part of the community. Some of them don’t have the pleasure of going to Northwestern or Rush, these fancy hospitals. The community deserves great nurses, but we keep losing nurses to Rush, Northwestern, UIC, and all these other places because St Mary’s cannot compete with them.” Brenda, also from St. Mary, added to this. “With the union, I know that we’re going to get support to fix our staffing grids, and hopefully to retain nurses. Nurses don’t want to do bedside anymore because of the working conditions. During COVID, everyone was a hero, right? All the nurses were heroes. Once that attention went away, they started cutting down. A lot of the things changed about two years ago when Prime took over, and healthcare is now for profit instead of to help our communities.” She further asserted that “healthcare should never bring profit for any company, any government, anything like that. It shouldn’t be a means of profit. In the end, unionization affects our community and affects our patients. With the strike and how much support we had from the community, it was because we’ve taken care of them. We’ve taken care of their kids, we’ve taken care of their families, and themselves. The community knows, and that’s why they were so appreciative and supportive of our movement.” Jesús was one of the multiple nurses that Prime Healthcare had fired during the campaign. Despite this, he shared, “I would still do the exact same thing because regardless of everything that happened, you get further together than just by yourself. We have to organize regardless of where you are, and what you do. At the end of the day you have to work together to make your workplace better. You and your coworkers have a voice which is something that the bosses don’t want you to have.” As was mentioned above, while the 20 percent overall unionization rate of nurses is impressive compared to the average workforce, there is still a lot of room to grow a labor movement of healthcare workers. The overall chronic terrible state of healthcare in this country means there is an ongoing potential to organize patients alongside unions to win significant reforms. A number of newly elected politicians won with a promise of winning healthcare for all. When the Democratic Party majority in Congress gets seated in January 2027, accompanying this event will be severe cuts to Medicaid as a result of Trump’s 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act. These changes will slash about 1 trillion dollars from health services over the next 10 years. Resisting austerity and fighting for the healthcare we deserve will take significant struggle and solidarity between workers and patients – hopefully, the recent victories of nurses in Chicago will help set the stage for successful fights.
